# Overview

In this lab, you will apply the principles of the Grammar of Graphics using the ggplot2 package. You will begin by working with a provided dataset to learn how visualizations are constructed and customized in R. You will then create visualizations using the dataset you have been working with throughout the course.

The goal of this lab is to develop your ability to communicate information visually while reinforcing the relationship between data structure, analytical questions, and graphical design.

Part 1: Exploring Visualizations with a Sample Dataset

For this section, provide students with a clean dataset from your package (perhaps phx_crime, tempe_hate, or tucson_bike).

Exercise 1: Create a Bar Chart

Create a bar chart showing the frequency of incidents by category.

Questions:

What categories occur most frequently?
What patterns stand out in the chart?
How does changing the order of categories affect interpretation?
Exercise 2: Create a Time Series Visualization

Aggregate incidents by month and create a line chart.

Questions:

Are incidents increasing or decreasing over time?
Do any seasonal patterns appear?
What additional information would help explain these patterns?
Exercise 3: Create a Distribution Plot

Create a histogram using a numeric variable.

Examples:

Victim age
Number of casualties
Property loss
Bicycle value

Questions:

Is the distribution symmetric or skewed?
Are there any unusual values?
What does the distribution suggest about the underlying data?
Exercise 4: Create a Comparative Visualization

Create a boxplot comparing a numeric variable across groups.

Examples:

Victim age by offense type
Bicycle value by neighborhood
Property loss by offense category

Questions:

Which groups have the highest median values?
Which groups exhibit the greatest variability?
Are there any notable outliers?
Exercise 5: Customize a Visualization

Choose one visualization from Exercises 1–4 and improve it by adding:

Informative title
Subtitle
Axis labels
Improved theme
Appropriate color choices

Questions:

What changes did you make?
How did the changes improve readability?
Part 2: Visualizing Your Own Dataset

Using the dataset you selected earlier in the course, create visualizations that address meaningful analytical questions.

Visualization 1: Distribution or Comparison

Create a visualization that shows either:

The distribution of a variable, or
A comparison between categories.

Examples:

Calls for service by type
Arrests by offense category
Incidents by neighborhood

Provide a brief interpretation (1–2 paragraphs).

Visualization 2: Trend Analysis

Create a visualization that examines change over time.

Examples:

Monthly incident counts
Yearly arrest totals
Calls for service by week

Provide a brief interpretation (1–2 paragraphs).

Visualization 3: Relationship Between Variables

Create a visualization showing a relationship between two variables.

Examples:

Scatterplot
Grouped bar chart
Faceted visualization

Provide a brief interpretation (1–2 paragraphs).

Submission Requirements

Submit:

Your completed R script (.R file)
A rendered HTML document generated with Quarto
Three visualizations from your own dataset
Written interpretations for each visualization

# How to Submit

Download the [template for this lab](../labs/templates/lab-04-LastName.zip?raw=true) prior to beginning the lab. 

<br>

### Knitting to HTML

When you have completed your assignment, click the "Knit" button to render your `.RMD` file into a `.HTML` report.

<br>

### Special Instructions

Upload your `.Rmd`, `.html`, and `.mp4` files to the appropriate link for this assignment on the Canvas page for this course.

<br>

### Before You Submit

Remember to ensure the following before submitting your assignment.

  * Name your files using this format: **Lab-04-LastName.Rmd**, **Lab-04-LastName.html**, and **Lab-04-LastName.mp4**.
  * Show both the solution for your code and write out your answers in the body text 

See [Google's R Style Guide](https://google.github.io/styleguide/Rguide.xml) for examples of common conventions.

<br>
<br>

### Common Knitting Issues

`.Rmd` files are knit into `.html` and other formats procedural, or line-by-line.

* An error in code when knitting will halt the process; error messages will tell you the specific line with the error
* Certain functions, like `install.packages()` or `setwd()`, are bound to cause errors in knitting 
* Altering a dataset or variable in one chunk will affect its use in all later chunks
* If an object is "not found", make sure it was created or loaded with `library()` in a previous chunk

**If All Else Fails:** If you cannot determine and fix the errors in a code chunk that's preventing you from knitting your document, add `eval = FALSE` inside the brackets of `{r}` at the beginning of a chunk to ensure that R does not attempt to evaluate it, that is: `{r eval = FALSE}`. This will prevent an erroneous chunk of code from halting the knitting process.
